explanations: luna: The section gives a secondary dictionary sense of loss in trade. This parable says the exchange of guidance for error did not profit its traders, using trade loss figuratively rather than for actual capital or debt. | terra: The exchange of guidance for error is said to be a trade that did not profit; it supplies the Qur'anic reversal of the section's dictionary sense “to be put down in one's trade,” a loss larger than capital.

terra: In a blood-liability settlement, any portion pardoned by the claimant is followed by fair pursuit and gracious payment, and the arrangement is explicitly called a lightening and mercy; it closely models a creditor reducing a quantified due without abolishing justice.

luna: The section names roots ʿ-s-r and y-s-r while applying their hardship/ease pair to restricted and ample means. In the fasting rule, God intends ease (al-yusr) rather than hardship (al-ʿusr); the same pair is used for bodily religious difficulty, a distinct sense from debt. | terra: God wills ٱلْيُسْرَ and not ٱلْعُسْرَ in the fasting law; the nonfinancial legal use clarifies that the financial narrowness in the section is one concrete instance of a broader divine preference for relief.
terra: Consuming one another's wealth wrongfully, including by manipulating judgment, marks the boundary between enforcing a lawful principal and exploiting a debtor's property.

luna: The section's cited expression measures voluntary charity by wealth left after dependents. Asked what to spend, this ayah answers al-ʿafw, the surplus, giving a direct Quranic counterpart to that measure. | terra: When asked what to spend, the answer is ٱلْعَفْوَ, the surplus; this directly matches the section's dictionary measure of charity as what remains beyond one's dependants.

terra: The father owes food and clothing on a fair basis, yet no soul is charged beyond its capacity; this supplies the dependants whose due is met before the section's surplus becomes voluntary charity.
terra: The divorce gift is assessed عَلَى ٱلْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُۥ وَعَلَى ٱلْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُۥ, making abundance and constraint measurable bases for a financial obligation just as in 65:7.

terra: A divorced woman's half-dowry remains due unless she or the holder of the marriage bond waives it, and waiving is nearer to piety; this is a precise financial claim voluntarily lowered by its owner.
terra: Divorced women have a fair provision as a due, continuing the same means-sensitive family obligations that 2:236 and 65:7 quantify.

luna: The section develops debt and then voluntary charity. This ayah calls spending for God's sake a good loan that is multiplied, using the same creditor-and-advance transaction image with God as the recipient. | terra: A voluntary outlay is cast as a “good loan” to God that He multiplies, while وَٱللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْصُطُ names constriction and expansion together; the human creditor's reduced claim thus enters a larger divine account.

luna: The section's creditor can turn a demand into release by forgiving the debt. This ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, giving a specific ethical boundary for aid that would otherwise harm or humiliate its recipient. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; it supplies the humane manner required when a creditor chooses relief rather than humiliating a distressed debtor.
terra: The giver must not cancel charity's value by reminders and hurt, a concrete warning against turning voluntary relief into another form of pressure on its recipient.
terra: Giving is to come from good earnings and produce, not defective property one would accept only reluctantly; charitable reduction is thus measured by honest value as well as amount.

luna: The section concerns restricted means and giving to a debtor in need. This ayah names poverty as the threat that can deter spending, then contrasts it with God's promise of forgiveness and bounty; it supplies the giver's side of the same pressure. | terra: Satan threatens poverty when one spends, whereas God promises forgiveness and bounty; it exposes the fear of an emptied hand that can stop a creditor from remitting a claim.

terra: The poor may appear self-sufficient because restraint keeps them from importunate asking; a creditor therefore cannot infer ease from silence when judging whether a debtor is truly in hardship.

luna: The section locates the debtor's relief just after the usury ruling. This ayah distinguishes permitted trade from forbidden usury, supplying the financial setting in which a lender may either claim an increase or ease the debtor's account. | terra: The surrounding passage distinguishes lawful trade from usury; that boundary prevents the section's commercial vocabulary of capital and loss from turning creditor profit into a justification for pressing the distressed debtor.

luna: The section hears the debt reduction as an act of charity. This ayah contrasts God erasing usury with increasing charities (ṣadaqāt), giving the image's waiving of a claim a clear opposite to extracting an increase. | terra: God effaces usurious gain and causes charities to grow, reversing an ordinary creditor's account: increase through debt is loss, while what is given away increases.

terra: Between the destruction of usury and the order to abandon its remainder, believers who give zakat are promised their reward, keeping charitable circulation beside the creditor's relinquished gain.

luna: The section places the debtor's respite after the prohibition of usury. This adjacent command to abandon the remaining usury frames the later instruction to wait for an insolvent debtor as a boundary against continuing to extract more. | terra: The creditor is ordered to abandon مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ ٱلرِّبَوٰٓا۟, the outstanding usurious balance; 2:279 defines the remaining lawful principal and 2:280 then addresses an insolvent debtor.

luna: The section turns 94:2 into a creditor's reduction of a debt. In this immediately surrounding debt ruling, a repentant lender keeps principal, with neither party wronging the other; that sets a precise limit on what may be claimed from a debtor. | terra: Repentance from usury leaves the creditor only رُءُوسُ أَمْوَالِكُمْ, the principal itself; this makes the section's measurable lowering of a claim precise and bars both creditor and debtor from injustice.

luna: The section names root ʿ-s-r for the debtor's restricted means and dictionary form al-maysara for abundance. This ayah stages that debtor directly: give time until ease, or forgive the debt as charity. | terra: This is the section's full creditor-debtor scene: ذُو عُسْرَةٍ is granted time إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ, while relinquishing the claim as charity is named the better course.

terra: Between debt relief and debt documentation comes the day when every soul is paid in full for what it earned; the placement turns the human account into a reminder of the final settlement without erasing 2:280's mercy.

luna: The section's dictionary form dhikr al-ḥaqq means a debt note; this ayah orders a term debt recorded and says one witness may remind the other (tadhakkira, root dh-k-r). It makes the ledger image literal. | terra: A debt due at a fixed term is to be written and witnessed, and فَتُذَكِّرَ إِحْدَىٰهُمَا ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ makes remembering part of preserving the claim; this is the Qur'anic realization of the section's “dhikr” as debt deed.

luna: The section connects remembrance to a written debt claim. Following the writing rule, this ayah handles a debt when no scribe is available through collateral and an entrusted borrower's duty to discharge the trust. | terra: Collateral, entrusted repayment, and the duty not to conceal testimony continue the written-debt scene of 2:282 and show how a claim is preserved when a scribe is unavailable.

luna: The section makes the weight lifted in 94:2 concrete through a written-off debt. This prayer asks not to have a burden laid on the community or what it cannot bear, and closes by asking pardon; its burden is moral, not financial. | terra: The final prayer joins capacity-limited obligation, a plea not to have a crushing burden laid upon the believers, and requests for pardon and forgiveness; these are the moral and bodily dimensions of the section's remitted liability in one ayah.

luna: The section stages a creditor and a borrower whose funds are entrusted or owed. This ayah contrasts a person who returns a large entrusted sum with one who will not return even a small coin unless pressed, making repayment and insistence on a claim concrete.

luna: The section's cited expression presents charity from wealth left after dependents. This ayah sets a more demanding measure: righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves, so the image opens from surplus toward costly generosity. | terra: Attaining righteousness requires spending from what one loves, extending the section's ordinary surplus measure by refusing to make generosity merely the disposal of what has little value.

luna: The section's debt scene turns on how a creditor treats an insolvent borrower. This prohibition of multiplied usury is a boundary against growing a claim through compounding it while the debtor is pressed. | terra: Usury that is multiplied again and again is the precise opposite of lowering a claim from an insolvent debtor's account.

luna: The section joins hardship, means, and charitable release. This ayah praises those who spend in both prosperity and adversity and pardon people, so it links giving across circumstances with the creditor's choice to forgive. | terra: Those praised spend in prosperity and adversity and pardon people; this extends the section's surplus-based measure by showing that generosity and relinquishment can remain virtues even in one's own straitness.

luna: The section describes charity drawn from a person's means and a burden lifted from the back. This ayah warns that wealth people withhold will be made a collar around their necks, a reversal in which retained wealth becomes a burden. | terra: What people withhold from God's bounty will be collared around them, turning retained surplus into a bodily burden rather than protected wealth.

terra: Women receive their dowries as an entitlement, but may willingly remit part of it; the ayah distinguishes a due from its freehearted cancellation exactly as the section distinguishes debt from charitable remission.

terra: The wealthy guardian must abstain from an orphan's property, the poor guardian may take reasonably, and witnesses attend its return; means, entrusted capital, and an accountable transfer meet here.

luna: The section names a deduction from capital and pictures a debt account. This inheritance rule allocates shares only after a bequest or debt is discharged, treating the debt as an amount settled before the remaining property is divided. | terra: Inheritance shares are distributed only after any bequest and debt; an outstanding debt is thus a quantifiable charge deducted from an estate before wealth reaches heirs.

luna: The section's creditor-debtor image concerns a claim against available property. This inheritance rule likewise calculates family shares after a bequest or debt, showing how a debt reduces the estate before distribution. | terra: The repeated priority of bequest and debt in the spouse and sibling shares shows the creditor's written claim surviving the debtor's death, a legal edge to the section's remissible burden.
terra: Mutually accepted trade is separated from consuming wealth wrongfully, supplying the transactional boundary needed beside the section's capital, loss, and creditor language.
terra: The responsibility of family maintenance is tied to spending from one's wealth, helping identify the dependent obligations that precede giving from surplus.
terra: Blood money must be delivered to the victim's family unless they relinquish it as charity, making the voluntary cancellation of a monetary liability itself ṣadaqah just as in 2:280.
terra: In the same family-law sphere as maintenance, separated spouses are each promised sufficiency from God's abundance, preventing present dependence from being treated as permanent.

luna: The section's creditor can use a claim either to press the insolvent or to release him. This ayah condemns taking usury despite its prohibition, a concrete opposite to easing the debt. | terra: The taking of usury and consuming people's wealth wrongfully are paired, placing creditor profit beyond principal on the unjust side of the section's scene.

luna: The section presents a debt as a measurable claim on property. This final inheritance rule again places bequests and debts before the division, a concrete legal instance of settling the account first.

luna: The section interprets 94:2 through a creditor's claim and a charitable waiver. This covenant ayah also uses the concrete phrase “lend God a good loan” for giving wealth; the lender's recipient and promised return differ from the section's human debt. | terra: A “good loan” to God is paired with almsgiving and answered by the erasure of wrongs, recasting voluntary expenditure as a debt whose divine creditor remits rather than presses.
terra: After fixing equivalent retaliation as a right, the ayah calls waiving that right as charity an expiation; a claimant's measurable entitlement can thus become charitable release.

terra: The expiatory meal is measured by the average of what one feeds one's own family, and inability triggers a nonfinancial alternative; it directly grounds giving in household support and actual means.

luna: The section's root ẓ-h-r names the back strained by a load. This verse pictures people carrying their burdens on their backs at judgment, a contrary bodily image that clarifies the section's movement from an imposed weight to release. | terra: Those who deny the meeting carry أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ, making liability a load on the back; the section's cancelled debt gives equally concrete measure to that load's removal.

luna: The section joins a strained back to a measurable financial load. This ayah requires full measure and just weight, then says God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity; together they set fair account and capacity beside the section's relieved burden. | terra: The ayah protects an orphan's property, commands full measure and weight with justice, and immediately limits responsibility to capacity, joining entrusted capital, an exact account, and means-sensitive obligation.

luna: The section's dictionary form waḍīʿa is a deduction from capital. In Shuʿayb's trade setting, this ayah forbids shortchanging people and requires full measure and weight, distinguishing a voluntary debt reduction from an unfair deduction in commerce. | terra: Shuʿayb commands full measure and weight and forbids diminishing people's possessions, a direct commercial boundary around the section's language of capital deduction.

luna: The section's wording waḍaʿnā ʿanka (root w-d-ʿ) is heard as a creditor laying down a claim; here the same root and ʿan construction say the messenger removes people's burden and fetters. The verse gives a direct image of release, though its burden is religious rather than financial. | terra: وَيَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ uses the same “put down from them” construction for removing a binding burden; it confirms the section's hearing of وَضَعْنَا عَنكَ as concrete release from liability.

terra: Commerce whose decline is feared is listed among possessions that can hold people back, supplying the section's secondary commercial-loss sense with an explicit human fear of shrinking capital.
terra: Those who fear poverty are promised enrichment from God's bounty, another explicit movement from anticipated scarcity to divine sufficiency.

luna: The section links wealth to giving and to a load on the back. This ayah condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending it in God's way; the next ayah turns that stored wealth into a bodily burden. | terra: Hoarded gold and silver are condemned precisely because they are not spent in God's path; retained surplus becomes culpable rather than safe capital.

luna: The section's debt image makes release of a load concrete, and its charity citation names the back of wealth. This continuation brands hoarded gold and silver onto backs at judgment, the reverse image of wealth given to relieve need. | terra: The hoarded wealth is heated and brands foreheads, sides, and ظُهُور; wealth withheld from giving becomes a load and mark on the very back invoked by the section.

luna: The section pictures a debtor in straits and a creditor who can ease that strait. This ayah names debtors (al-ghārimīn) among the recipients of obligatory charity, joining debt relief to provision for people in need. | terra: Alms are assigned explicitly to ٱلْغَٰرِمِينَ, people burdened by debt, turning charitable giving into direct relief of the section's debtor.
terra: The mockers deride donors who can find only their utmost effort; the ayah protects sincere giving from scarce means and marks the limit of judging charity only by surplus size.

luna: The section centers someone unable to pay because of straitened means. In the adjacent campaign passage, this ayah excuses the weak, sick and those who cannot find what to spend when they are sincere; it makes inability to provide a real limiting condition.

luna: The section attends to the embarrassment of a person in material straits. This adjacent ayah describes people who cannot find mounts to go with the army turning away with tears because they have nothing to spend, a specific scene of inability rather than unwillingness.
terra: Some Bedouins treat what they spend as مَغْرَمًا, an imposed financial loss or liability; this is the resentful opposite of freely turning a claim into charity.

luna: The section names root ʿ-s-r for distress, especially lack of means. This ayah calls the Tabuk campaign the hour of hardship (sāʿat al-ʿusra), using the same hardship word for a collective, resource-strained trial rather than a private debt.

luna: The section's dictionary note also applies the root w-d-ʿ to commercial loss. Shuʿayb tells prosperous traders not to decrease measure or weight; the verse makes a commercial reduction an injustice rather than the generous write-off in the section. | terra: Shuʿayb sees his people in prosperity yet warns them not to diminish measure or weight, showing that abundance can produce oppressive accounting rather than merciful relief.

luna: The section's dictionary form waḍīʿa means an amount taken off capital. This continuation requires full measure and forbids depriving people of their goods, marking the contrast between an unfair shortfall and a creditor's voluntary reduction. | terra: The command to give full measure and weight with justice and not deprive people of their goods completes the fair-account scene begun in 11:84.

terra: Joseph's brothers arrive with بِبِضَٰعَةٍ مُّزْجَىٰةٍ, deficient purchasing capital, and ask him both to give full measure and to treat them charitably; scarcity, trade, and voluntary remission meet in one scene.
terra: God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it tightly, while worldly abundance is only a brief enjoyment; this relativizes both parties' present positions in the debt scene.

luna: The section explicitly likens its verses to a ledger and says a debt instrument may be called a remembrance. This ayah introduces each person's opened book at resurrection, a divine record rather than a creditor's note; 17:14 tells the person to read it and calls him his own reckoner.

luna: The section's ledger image grows from the debt note it associates with remembrance. This ayah's own contribution is to make the person read his record and serve as his own reckoner; 17:13 supplies the opened book that it continues.
terra: Kin, the needy, and the traveler are to receive their due before the warning against waste; it helps specify the prior claims on wealth behind the section's reference to dependants.

luna: The section describes short means as little in the hand and ends with the hand emptying or filling. This ayah pictures a hand bound to the neck or stretched out completely, then marks a measured course between withholding and exhausting one's means. | terra: The hand may be neither chained to the neck nor extended completely; it gives the section's “back of wealth” rule a Qur'anic boundary between miserliness and spending that leaves the giver destitute.

terra: Immediately after the rule against a clenched or wholly outspread hand, God is said to expand and restrict provision; the giver's limit is placed inside the divine movement between width and scarcity.

luna: The section extends debt reduction into the image of an account being adjusted. This ayah requires full measure and just weight in trade, a boundary showing that lowering someone's debt is relief, while lowering their due goods is injustice. | terra: Full measure and weighing with a straight balance state the commercial fairness that must govern the creditor's calculation before any voluntary remission begins.
terra: The ruined garden owner turns his palms over what he spent on it, giving the section's “loss in trade” a visible scene of capital irretrievably gone.

luna: The section explicitly reads its first verses as an account ledger and connects remembrance to a written debt claim. This ayah presents a different ledger, a record that leaves no small or great deed uncounted; the link is the record-and-account image, not a human debt. | terra: وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ places the comprehensive record before its debtors, while nothing small or great is omitted; it is a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the section's account book made concrete by وضع.
terra: Just balances are set for resurrection and even a mustard-seed weight is brought forward, giving the section's account book an exact standard of measure.

luna: The section describes a person with means choosing whether to ease another's hardship. This ayah addresses people of bounty and abundance, tells them not to withhold from relatives and the needy, and calls them to pardon and overlook, meeting both abundance and forgiveness. | terra: People of bounty and abundance are told to continue giving to vulnerable kin and to pardon and overlook; material width and relinquishing a due are joined as the creditor's generous stance.
terra: The poor who marry are promised enrichment from God's bounty, another concrete promise that present lack of means need not remain permanent.

terra: An enslaved person who seeks a written emancipation contract is to receive one when good is known, and the holder must give from God's wealth; a binding written liability is answered by material help from the party with power.
luna: The section uses al-ʿusr for restricted means, while this ayah calls the Day of Judgment ʿasīr, difficult for the deniers; the shared root carries difficulty beyond the financial sense.

luna: The section's charity citation measures giving from what remains after dependents. This ayah describes the servants' spending between extravagance and stinginess, making moderation a specific counterpart to that measure. | terra: Righteous spending is neither extravagant nor stingy but proportionate between them, another Qur'anic measure for the section's charity from available means.

luna: The section cites waḍīʿa, a reduction from capital, as part of its financial image. Shuʿayb's command to give full measure begins a repeated warning against reducing what is owed to another. | terra: Giving full measure and not joining those who cause loss establishes the fair commercial baseline from which the section's claimant may freely reduce his own right.

luna: The section's debt image depends on a measured amount being removed from an account. This next command requires weighing with a straight balance, completing the commercial measure whose deliberate reduction is condemned in this passage. | terra: Weighing with a straight balance supplies the exact instrument for the account continued from 26:181.

luna: The section distinguishes a generous write-off from loss in commerce. This continuation forbids depriving people of their goods, giving the moral difference between reducing another's claim for their relief and shortchanging them. | terra: Diminishing other people's goods is forbidden, distinguishing wrongful subtraction from lowering one's own claim for a debtor's benefit.

terra: After Qarun and his house are swallowed, the onlookers recognize that God expands and restricts provision; it stages an abrupt movement from conspicuous wealth to loss behind the section's lexical definition of entering hardship.
terra: God's expansion and restriction of provision for His servants gives the section's financial width and narrowness a repeated providential frame.
terra: The alternation of expanded and restricted provision is called a sign, reinforcing that the debtor's present scarcity is a condition that can change rather than a fixed identity.

luna: The section brings a debt claim beside voluntary charity. This ayah contrasts wealth given as usury to grow people's property with zakat given seeking God, a direct monetary contrast between extraction and charitable giving. | terra: What is given as usury to grow through people's wealth does not grow with God, whereas zakat is multiplied; apparent account-book gain and charitable decrease exchange outcomes.
terra: God alone expands and restricts provision, challenging the wealthy person's assumption that possession itself secures status in the section's creditor-debtor relation.
terra: God expands or restricts provision, and whatever the addressee spends He replaces; this directly answers the section's tension between giving from one's means and fear of diminished capital.
terra: All people are described as poor toward God while God alone is the Rich, placing the human creditor's temporary abundance inside a deeper debtor-like dependence.

terra: A heavily burdened soul may call for help, yet none of its load is carried even by close kin; the boundary clarifies that merciful cancellation removes a liability rather than merely transferring its weight.
terra: Generous recitation, prayer, and spending are called a trade that will never perish, the positive reversal of the section's commercial loss.
terra: God pays such traders their rewards in full and adds from His bounty, answering diminished worldly capital with an undiminished divine settlement.
terra: The repeated sign of provision expanded or measured tightly keeps both creditor abundance and debtor hardship contingent on God.
terra: The record is set down for judgment and the matter is settled justly; like 18:49, وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَٰبُ links the section's named root with an actual ledger.
terra: The One who owns the keys of heaven and earth expands and restricts provision; the parties' unequal hands are located within a larger ownership than their private account.
terra: God sends down the Book with truth and the balance, another pairing of written authority and measured judgment relevant to an accurately reduced claim.
terra: Unlimited expansion of provision would make people transgress, so God sends it in due measure; this gives a boundary to the section's equation of width with desirable relief.
terra: Although an injured party may claim an equivalent return, one who pardons and repairs has reward with God; it supplies the general claimant's ethic behind forgiving part of a debt.
terra: حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا joins the section's verb “put down” to its burden noun: even war ends by laying down its loads.

terra: Those called to spend may withhold, but their stinginess harms themselves; God is the Rich while they are the poor, reversing the apparent wealth hierarchy between creditor and needy recipient.
terra: The beggar and deprived person possess a “right” in the generous person's wealth; beside the creditor's documented right, the section thus reveals a counterclaim made by need itself.

terra: The question whether the messenger demands payment so that people are مِن مَّغْرَمٍ مُّثْقَلُونَ depicts an assessed debt as an actual crushing weight, precisely joining the section's debt and burden images.
terra: وَأَنَّهُۥ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes enrichment and sufficiency to God, echoing the agent of the addressee's change from poverty in 93:8.
luna: The section names al-ʿusr for the strain of a debtor. This ayah calls the gathering day ʿasīr, a difficult day, using the same hardship word outside the financial setting.

luna: The section names al-yusr as abundance and dhikr as the remembrance associated with a debt note. This refrain says God made the Qur'an easy for remembrance (yassarnā ... li-l-dhikr), bringing both named roots together in different senses: ease of recitation and remembrance of revelation.

luna: The section names roots y-s-r and dh-k-r for ease/abundance and remembrance. This repeated refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, a distinct meeting of the two roots from the section's economic and debt-note senses.

luna: The section names roots y-s-r and dh-k-r for ease/abundance and remembrance. This repeated refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, a distinct meeting of the two roots from the section's economic and debt-note senses.

luna: The section names roots y-s-r and dh-k-r for ease/abundance and remembrance. This repeated refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, a distinct meeting of the two roots from the section's economic and debt-note senses.
terra: The sky is raised and the balance is set down: وَرَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ pairs the section's raising and lowering verbs with an instrument of exact accounting.
terra: The command not to transgress in the balance states the ethical limit governing the account whose scale is set down in 55:7.
terra: Upholding weight with justice and not diminishing the balance gives exact commercial content to the section's image of a claim being measured and reduced.
terra: People are told to spend from wealth over which God made them successors, weakening a creditor's claim to absolute ownership of the surplus he can use for relief.

luna: The section's debt scene makes a financial claim tangible. This ayah calls giving to God a good loan and promises its multiplication; the lender is God-directed rather than a human creditor, a distinct but concrete use of the same transaction image. | terra: The good loan to God is multiplied and rewarded generously, reversing the loss feared when capital leaves the giver's hand.

luna: The section links debt and charity. This ayah places men and women giving charity beside those who lend God a good loan, then promises multiplication, joining the two practices the section brings together. | terra: Men and women who give charity are themselves described as lending God a good loan, so charitable release and a creditor-debtor account are explicitly fused.
terra: The Book and balance are sent so people may uphold justice, placing written claims and measured settlement under the same norm as the section's debt ledger.

luna: The section's cited expression measures charity from abundance left after dependents. This ayah praises people who prefer others even when they themselves have need (khaṣāṣa), a specific case beyond the surplus measure. | terra: The Helpers prefer others despite privation in themselves, a specific exceptional generosity beyond the section's ordinary measure of giving from surplus.
terra: The offer of a trade that saves from punishment introduces a profitable divine transaction, reversing the section's image of loss in ordinary commerce.
terra: That saving trade requires expenditure of wealth as well as personal striving, so capital apparently put down becomes the price of enduring gain.
terra: Forgiveness and gardens are the settlement of the trade described in 61:10-11, completing its reversal of commercial loss.
terra: At death the person asks for a brief delay so that he can give charity; this reverses 2:280, where the living creditor can grant a debtor time and turn the claim itself into charity.
terra: God will not delay a soul once its term arrives, marking the absolute boundary against which a human creditor's merciful extension in 2:280 is meaningful.

luna: The section connects generosity with relief of financial strain. This ayah urges spending and praises freedom from stinginess; 64:17 follows by expressing giving as a good loan to God. | terra: People are told to be mindful as far as they are able and to spend, while guarding against their own stinginess; 64:17 immediately recasts that spending as a good loan multiplied by God.

luna: The section hears a cancelled human claim as charity. This ayah describes giving as a good loan to God, to be multiplied and forgiven, a specific reversal in which the divine creditor repays the giver with increase and pardon. | terra: If people lend God a good loan, He multiplies it and forgives them; increase and remission occupy the same divine account that the section evokes.

luna: The section names root y-s-r for ease and cites 65:7's support rule. Earlier in the same divorce passage, this ayah promises ease in one's affairs to the God-fearing; 65:6–7 then gives the concrete maintenance and spending rules, so its ease promise belongs to that setting. | terra: Within the same divorce legislation, God makes ease in the affair of one who is mindful; 65:7 then gives that ease a specifically financial form after hardship.

luna: The section places 65:7's spending-by-means rule in divorce maintenance. This preceding ayah gives the concrete case: provide for pregnant divorced women until birth and pay them for nursing, so the following rule has an actual household obligation in view. | terra: The payer must house and maintain the women according to his means and must not pressure them to constrict them; 65:7 then specifies spending by abundance or restricted provision.

luna: The section connects al-ʿusr and al-yusr with a change in means. This ayah orders spending according to one's means and promises ease after hardship (ʿusr, root ʿ-s-r; yusr, root y-s-r), in the same divine voice. | terra: Support is scaled to actual means—ذُو سَعَةٍ from his abundance and the person whose provision is restricted from what God gave him—before the exact promise that God will make ease after hardship.
terra: This repeated question likewise pictures an demanded fee as a debt under which the addressees are weighed down, giving bodily force to the liability lifted in the section.
terra: The worshippers recognize a known right in their wealth, converting surplus from mere possession into an accounted obligation.
terra: That known right belongs to the petitioner and deprived, completing the reversal in which the person with means is also a debtor to the person in need.

luna: The section links charity to its debt image. In a passage about prayer, alms and people's acts, this ayah also calls giving to God a good loan, a separate but explicit use of lending language for voluntary provision. | terra: The good loan is sent ahead and found with God better and greater in reward, making apparently reduced present wealth a credit preserved in another ledger.
luna: The section names root ʿ-s-r for a debtor's hardship. Here ʿasīr names the difficult Day of Judgment, extending that root from material straits to an ultimate trial rather than a debt.
luna: The section names al-yusr for ease alongside al-ʿusr for hardship. This next ayah says that day will not be easy for the deniers, completing the judgment-day reversal begun in 74:9.

luna: The section's dictionary form waḍīʿa means a reduction from capital, and it mentions loss in trade. This ayah curses short-measurers, introducing the opposite case: reducing what is due to another is wrongdoing, not debt relief. | terra: The warning to those who defraud introduces the opposite creditor-merchant posture from charitable reduction: an account is manipulated for the stronger party's gain.

luna: The section discusses trade loss and lowering an amount. This continuation says the short-measurer takes full measure for himself, showing the creditor's self-favoring side of an unjust account; 83:3 completes the under-measuring side. | terra: The defrauders demand full measure when receiving for themselves, the inverse of the creditor who voluntarily accepts less from a distressed debtor.

luna: The section's debt reduction is presented as a way to ease another's strait. This continuation says the short-measurer gives less when measuring for others, the contrary act of imposing a loss instead of forgiving one. | terra: When giving by measure or weight, they cause others loss; this distinguishes imposed diminution of another's right from the claimant's own charitable remission.
terra: Receiving one's book in the right hand supplies the document immediately before the “easy account” of 84:8; the cited ayah contributes the favorable ledger and hand.
terra: حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا is literally an easy reckoning, bringing the section's y-s-r promise and its account-book hearing into the same phrase.
terra: Joyful return to one's people is the outcome of the easy account in 84:8, completing the release rather than the calculation itself.
terra: The person given his book from behind his back reverses the joyful easy account of 84:7-9; the section's back and ledger images meet on the adverse side of reckoning.
terra: The recipient of the book behind his back calls for destruction, supplying the debtor-like dread on the adverse side of the account begun in 84:10.
terra: Entering the blaze completes the consequence of that adverse ledger; this row contributes the enforced settlement, while 84:10 contributes the book behind the back.

luna: The section explicitly separates the abundance sense of al-maysara from the ease sense of y-s-r. This promise that God will ease the Prophet toward the easier way uses the latter sense and the same divine voice as the surah's promise of ease. | terra: وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ is another divine promise of ease to the prophetic addressee, supporting the personal promise heard through the section's financial sense of yusr.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for al-ʿusr is restricted means and its counterword al-maysara is abundance. This ayah pictures a person receiving plentiful provision and mistaking it for honor, setting up the exact wealth contrast continued in the next ayah. | terra: A person reads expanded provision as proof that God has honored him; 89:16 exposes the matching interpretation of restricted provision, and the passage rejects wealth as that simple moral account.

luna: The section describes a person falling from plenty into straitened means. This next ayah says a person mistakes restricted provision for humiliation; the continuation in 89:17–20 turns to neglected orphans and feeding the poor, giving the economic contrast an ethical consequence. | terra: When provision is measured tightly, the person says God has humiliated him; the section instead hears hardship beside promised ease, not as a final verdict on worth.

luna: The section joins straitened means to a creditor's choice to relieve a vulnerable person. After the preceding ayah's contrast between ample and restricted provision, this ayah says people fail to honor the orphan; 89:18 continues with failure to urge feeding the poor. | terra: The correction to the mistaken wealth judgments in 89:15-16 begins with failure to honor the orphan, showing how abundance is tested by treatment of the vulnerable.

luna: The section's debt image asks the reader to see a person in need as someone who can be relieved. This ayah's own contribution is the failure to urge feeding the poor, continuing the social response to restricted provision begun in 89:17. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the poor gives the concrete social consequence of reading restricted provision as humiliation rather than a claim on the community's means.
terra: Greedily consuming inheritance adds an account-book wrong: the powerful take another's assigned wealth instead of preserving or relinquishing their own claim.
terra: Excessive love of wealth completes the diagnosis behind harshness toward the poor and reluctance to lower a financial claim.
terra: Feeding on a day of hunger makes material straitness itself the setting for generosity, another qualified extension beyond giving only in ease.
terra: The near orphan is the first recipient named in that hunger scene, keeping family vulnerability inside the giver's calculation.
terra: The destitute person in the dust completes the scene of aid directed to the most visibly constricted condition.

luna: The section imagines a creditor turning a claim into charity. This ayah's own contribution is the person who gives, is mindful of God, and affirms the good; 92:7 completes the image by describing ease for that course. | terra: The branch leading to ease begins with the person who gives and is mindful; 92:7 names the resulting “ease,” so generosity occupies the creditor's side of the section's choice.

luna: The section pairs want and abundance through roots ʿ-s-r and y-s-r. In this surah's account of giving and withholding, God makes the generous, God-conscious person easy for the easy course (al-yusrā); here the ease is a moral path rather than wealth. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward ease after the giving of 92:5, joining the y-s-r root to openhanded conduct.

luna: The section describes the creditor's choice to ease a debtor in straits. This ayah supplies the contrary disposition: a person withholds and deems himself self-sufficient; 92:10 completes that road with hardship. | terra: The counterfigure withholds and deems himself self-sufficient; 92:10 sends him toward hardship, reversing the creditor whose abundance becomes relief for another.

luna: The section's dictionary form al-maysara means abundance, while its root y-s-r also carries ease. In the same surah, the miser who treats himself as self-sufficient is eased toward hardship (al-ʿusrā), a reversal of the section's debtor receiving time and a creditor's possible generosity. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ turns the section's paired roots into a moral reversal: withholding and imagined self-sufficiency lead toward hardship rather than away from it.
terra: His wealth does not avail him when he falls, setting a boundary on the imagined security of the retained capital described in 92:8.
terra: The one who gives his wealth to purify himself embodies the freely given charity that, in the section, can take the form of cancelling a debtor's claim.

luna: The section explicitly recalls the previous surah's wording: God found the Prophet poor (ʿāʾilan) and enriched him (aghna). That remembered change from want to sufficiency fills out its empty-to-full-hand image. | terra: The same divine addressee was found عَآئِلًا and enriched; it supplies the section's concrete movement from an empty hand to financial sufficiency.
terra: After the addressee is reminded that God enriched him, he is forbidden to subdue the orphan; received abundance is thus made a reason not to exercise power harshly over someone vulnerable.
terra: The same enriched addressee must not repel the petitioner, closely matching the creditor stance of not pressing or humiliating the person whose hand is empty.
terra: The addressee is to recount his Lord's favor after being enriched; his fuller hand remains a remembered gift rather than self-owned proof of superiority over the debtor.
terra: Harshly repelling the orphan is a social counterpart to the creditor who presses someone without power; it supplies a specific condemned posture toward vulnerability.
terra: Refusal even to urge feeding the poor completes the withholding posture introduced in 107:2 and opposes remission as charity.
